final.title: Why subscription sprawl survives in small teams
final.body:
Subscription sprawl survives in small teams because it gets treated as background admin. Someone signs up for a tool, the renewal date lives in an inbox or a card statement, and the cleanup keeps slipping behind invoices, email, and the work that feels more urgent. The problem is usually visibility before it is software.

For an owner-operator, the useful question is simple: can you list every active subscription and its renewal date right now? If not, the first step is not automation. It is a one-time manual audit so you have a clean list. If yes, the next step is to decide whether the list should stay as a spreadsheet or become a controlled workflow that sends renewal reminders and flags odd charges for human review.

That is the kind of bounded workflow Bareni looks for: one recurring task, one owner, one clear control, and no forcing AI into the wrong place. If the list is already tidy and small, a spreadsheet may be enough. If it is messy, start with the audit, then decide whether a simple AI-assisted workflow is worth building. Human approval still stays in charge for any cancellation or payment step.

final.title: Why subscription sprawl survives in small teams
final.body:
Subscription sprawl usually survives in small teams because it gets treated as background admin. A tool is signed up for, the renewal date is noted somewhere, and then the note gets buried under invoices, emails, and everything else that was already waiting.

For an owner-operator, the real workflow decision is simple: do you have one place where every active subscription and renewal date is visible, or is the knowledge spread across inboxes and memory? If it is spread out, the first step is not automation. It is a one-time manual audit so you can build a clean list first. That is the kind of bounded workflow Bareni looks for: one recurring task, one clear owner, and a control that fits the actual mess in front of you. Human approval still owns any cancellation or payment step. Tiny bit of unglamorous work, but that is often the point.
